other_side: The edition's lead is that a White House turf battle will decide which AI you can use, with OpenAI's Dean Ball wanting to smother cheap Chinese open-weight rivals through manufactured regulatory fear because they 'deter AI CapEx' and undercut premium frontier demand. Zitron's counter is that the reason OpenAI needs regulators to kneecap cheap open-weight competition is simpler and less noble than national security: its premium business is a money-losing bubble that commoditisation would expose. He calls OpenAI "one of the largest liabilities in recent economic history," notes it intends to burn over $852 billion by 2030 with no tangible return, and argues that without OpenAI "the justification for trillions of dollars of capex evaporates." On his reading, Ball's 'decelerationist' and 'communist' framing of open weights is an incumbent defending an unsustainable monopoly against products that reveal the emperor has no clothes.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is whether premium frontier AI has durable economic value, or whether cheap open-weight models commoditise it to nothing. Both accept the same facts: open weights are getting good enough and far cheaper, and OpenAI is spending staggering sums to stay ahead. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the premium tier earns returns that survive commoditisation; the observable that settles it is OpenAI's audited revenue against its costs, and whether enterprises keep paying a real premium over free weights once the fear subsides. The residue is worldview: NLW reads a live policy fight worth tracking, Zitron a bubble that regulation is being recruited to prop up. NLW is vindicated if frontier labs show sustainable margins even as open weights improve; Zitron if losses mount while open models close the gap. Both are polemicists with incentives - NLW bullish and anti-doom for an audience of buyers, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype for paying subscribers - so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: compute and capital, not benchmarks, will set the terms. Watch OpenAI's next funding round and burn rate.
